greeting: Hello{name_suffix}! How can I help you today?
Hi{name_suffix}! What would you like to know?
goodbye: Bye{name_suffix}, it was good talking with you.
how_are_you: I am running well and ready to help. How are you?
All systems are working fine. What can I do for you?
I am doing great, thanks for asking. What is on your mind?
identity: I am Solen 1.0, a small AI built from two connected models: a neural brain that understands your question and a language model that writes the answer.
My name is Solen 1.0. I am an AI with my own neural network and my own language model, trained on basic knowledge.
capabilities: I know about 480 facts, with a specialty in building AI models: data, training, neural network architectures, language models, evaluation, tools and deployment. I also cover science, math, geography, history, computing, health and language. I can also build small AI models for you. Just describe what you want, for example: make me an AI that predicts house prices from data/examples/houses.csv. I can build text and table classifiers, number predictors with custom network designs, chatbots, document Q&A models, summarizers, translators, a small transformer (mini GPT), text generators, image classifiers, image generators, audio classifiers, clustering models, anomaly detectors, forecasters, recommenders and maze-solving reinforcement learning agents. For models that need GPU clusters, like ChatGPT or video generators, I explain why and build the closest small version. Run them with /ask name input and list them with /models. I can also do arithmetic, remember your name, learn new facts with /teach question | answer, and write text with /generate <words>.
creator: I was built in the BuildYourModel project: a neural network brain plus a custom language model, written from scratch in Python and NumPy.
set_name: Great to meet you, {name}. I will remember that.
Hello {name}, I will remember your name.
get_name: You told me your name is {name}.
joke: Why do programmers prefer dark mode? Because light attracts bugs.
I told my computer I needed a break, and it said no problem, it will go to sleep.
Why was the math book sad? It had too many problems.
What do you call a fake noodle? An impasta.
affirm: Great! What would you like to know next?
deny: Okay. You can teach me the right answer with /teach question | answer.
Alright. Tell me what you meant and I will try again.

fact:284: A large language model is a neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, which lets it answer questions and write text.
fact:285: Vitamins are nutrients the body needs in small amounts to work properly. Most come from a varied diet of fruits, vegetables, grains and proteins.
fact:286: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps heal wounds. Oranges, strawberries, peppers and broccoli are good sources.
fact:287: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for strong bones. Skin makes it in sunlight, and it is also in fish, eggs and fortified milk.
fact:288: Protein builds and repairs muscles and tissues. Meat, fish, eggs, beans, lentils, nuts and dairy are good sources.
fact:289: Carbohydrates are the body's main source of energy. Whole grains, fruits, vegetables and beans are healthy sources.
fact:290: A calorie is a unit of energy from food. Many adults need roughly 2,000 to 2,500 calories a day, depending on size and activity.
fact:291: The brain controls thinking, memory, movement and the senses. It has about 86 billion neurons that send signals to each other.
fact:292: Adults usually have 32 teeth, including wisdom teeth. Children have 20 baby teeth.
fact:293: Blood carries oxygen, nutrients and immune cells. It has red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma. The main blood types are A, B, AB and O.
fact:294: Normal body temperature is about 37 degrees Celsius, or 98.6 Fahrenheit. A temperature of 38 Celsius or higher is usually considered a fever.
fact:295: A normal resting heart rate for adults is about 60 to 100 beats per minute.
fact:296: Blood pressure is the force of blood against artery walls. A healthy reading is around 120 over 80 or lower.
fact:297: The immune system defends the body against germs using white blood cells, antibodies and organs like the spleen and lymph nodes.
fact:298: A vaccine trains the immune system to recognize a germ without causing the disease, so the body can fight it off quickly later.
fact:299: Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, scrubbing all surfaces, then rinse and dry.
fact:300: Stress is the body's reaction to pressure. Exercise, good sleep, deep breathing, time outdoors and talking with people you trust can help reduce it.
fact:301: Digestion breaks food into nutrients. It starts in the mouth, continues in the stomach with acids, and nutrients are absorbed mostly in the small intestine.
fact:302: The five traditional senses are sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch.
fact:303: The liver filters toxins from the blood, makes bile to digest fat, and stores energy and vitamins.
fact:304: The kidneys filter waste and extra water from the blood to make urine, and help control blood pressure.
fact:305: The human body has about 600 muscles. The masseter, the jaw muscle, is often called the strongest for its size.
fact:306: Diabetes is a condition where blood sugar is too high because the body does not make enough insulin or cannot use it well. Insulin is a hormone that moves sugar into cells.
fact:307: A pronoun replaces a noun, such as he, she, they, it, we or you.
fact:308: A preposition shows how words relate in place or time, such as in, on, under, before or with.
fact:309: A conjunction joins words or sentences, such as and, but, or, because and so.
fact:310: A synonym has the same or similar meaning as another word, like big and large. An antonym has the opposite meaning, like hot and cold.
fact:311: Homophones sound the same but have different meanings or spellings, like there, their and they're.
fact:312: A simile compares using like or as, such as brave as a lion. A metaphor says one thing is another, such as time is money.
fact:313: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea, usually starting with a topic sentence.
fact:314: Punctuation marks make writing clear. Periods end sentences, commas separate parts, question marks end questions, and exclamation marks show strong feeling.
fact:315: A plural means more than one. Most English words add s or es, like cats or boxes, but some change, like child to children.
fact:316: Verb tenses show when something happens: past, like walked, present, like walk, and future, like will walk.
fact:317: A haiku is a short Japanese style poem with three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables.
fact:318: Consonants are the letters that are not vowels, like B, C, D and F. English has 21 consonant letters.
fact:319: Hello is hola in Spanish, bonjour in French, hallo in German, ciao in Italian, konnichiwa in Japanese and ni hao in Mandarin.
fact:320: Thank you is gracias in Spanish, merci in French, danke in German, grazie in Italian and arigato in Japanese.
fact:321: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like level, racecar or the number 121.
fact:322: An acronym is a word made from the first letters of other words, like NASA for National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
fact:323: A syllable is a single unit of sound in a word. Water has two syllables: wa and ter.
fact:324: Money is something people accept in exchange for goods and services. Inflation is when prices rise over time, so money buys less.
fact:325: A government runs a country. In a democracy, citizens choose their leaders by voting.
fact:326: An economy is how a place produces, sells and uses goods and services. GDP measures the total value of everything a country produces.
fact:327: The Olympic Games are an international sports competition held every four years, with Summer and Winter Games two years apart.
fact:328: A soccer team has 11 players on the field, including the goalkeeper.
fact:329: A basketball team has 5 players on the court at a time.
fact:330: Soccer, also called football, is the most popular sport in the world.
fact:331: Chess is a two player strategy game on an 8 by 8 board. Each player starts with 16 pieces, and the goal is checkmate, trapping the other king.
fact:332: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
fact:333: The giraffe is the tallest animal, growing up to about 5.5 meters tall.
fact:334: The ostrich is the largest bird. It cannot fly but can run about 70 kilometers per hour.
fact:335: The whale shark is the largest fish, reaching around 12 to 18 meters long. It eats plankton.
fact:336: Bees collect nectar to make honey and pollinate plants, which helps many fruits and crops grow.
fact:337: Giant pandas eat mostly bamboo, up to about 12 to 38 kilograms a day. They live in the mountains of central China.
fact:338: The Greenland shark is the longest living known vertebrate, possibly living about 400 years. Some sponges and corals live even longer.
fact:339: Global average life expectancy is about 73 years, and it varies a lot between countries.
fact:340: There are 100 centimeters in a meter and 1,000 meters in a kilometer.
fact:341: There are 1,000 grams in a kilogram and 1,000 kilograms in a metric ton.
fact:342: There are 12 inches in a foot, 3 feet in a yard and 5,280 feet in a mile.
fact:343: One mile is about 1.609 kilometers, and one kilometer is about 0.621 miles.
fact:344: To convert Celsius to Fahrenheit, multiply by 9/5 and add 32. To convert back, subtract 32 and multiply by 5/9.
fact:345: Music is organized sound with rhythm, melody and harmony. Western music uses seven note names: A, B, C, D, E, F and G.
fact:346: Dogs are domesticated mammals descended from wolves. They usually live about 10 to 13 years, depending on breed.
fact:347: Cats are small domesticated carnivores. They usually live about 12 to 18 years and sleep around 12 to 16 hours a day.
fact:348: To be more productive, set clear goals, work on one task at a time, take short breaks, limit distractions and get enough sleep.
fact:349: Study in short focused sessions, test yourself instead of rereading, space out your reviews over days and teach the idea to someone else.
fact:350: To build an AI model: 1, define the problem and what a good result looks like. 2, collect data. 3, clean and label it. 4, split it into training, validation and test sets. 5, start with a simple baseline model. 6, train a better model. 7, evaluate it on the test set. 8, tune hyperparameters. 9, deploy it. 10, monitor it and retrain as data changes.
fact:351: Start with Python, then learn NumPy and pandas, basic linear algebra, calculus and probability. Next learn scikit-learn for classic models, then PyTorch for neural networks. Build small projects early, like a spam filter or digit classifier, and grow from there.
fact:352: The key math for machine learning is linear algebra for vectors and matrices, calculus for gradients, probability and statistics for uncertainty and evaluation. You can start building with basic algebra and learn the rest as you go.
fact:353: Python is the main language for AI because of libraries like PyTorch, TensorFlow, scikit-learn, NumPy and Hugging Face. C++ and CUDA are used for high performance parts, and JavaScript for running models in browsers.
fact:354: It depends on size. A small classifier can train in seconds on a laptop, like my brain does. A medium deep learning model can take hours on a GPU. Large language models take weeks or months on thousands of GPUs.
fact:355: Small models cost almost nothing to train on your own computer or free tools like Google Colab. Fine-tuning a model can cost a few dollars to a few hundred. Training the largest language models from scratch can cost tens to hundreds of millions of dollars.
fact:356: Yes. No-code tools like Google Teachable Machine, cloud AutoML services and some Hugging Face tools let you train models by uploading data. Coding gives you much more control, though.
fact:357: I have two connected models. My brain is a neural network: hashed word and letter features go through an embedding layer, a hidden layer and a softmax, trained with Adam, dropout and data augmentation, backed by a TF-IDF retriever. My language model is a trigram model with Kneser-Ney smoothing that picks and fills my defined responses.
fact:358: Common model types are linear models, decision trees and forests, nearest neighbors, support vector machines, neural networks such as CNNs, RNNs and transformers, and generative models such as GANs, diffusion models and language models.
fact:359: Training data is the set of examples a model learns from. For supervised learning, each example has an input, like a sentence, and a label, like its category.
fact:360: It depends on the task. Simple classifiers can work with a few hundred examples per class. Deep image models often need thousands per class. Using a pretrained model and fine-tuning greatly reduces how much data you need.
fact:361: Good dataset sources are Kaggle, Hugging Face Datasets, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, Google Dataset Search, OpenML and government open data portals.
fact:362: Data cleaning means removing duplicates, fixing or removing missing values, correcting wrong labels, standardizing formats and removing outliers or junk. Clean data often matters more than a fancier model.
fact:363: Data labeling means attaching the correct answer to each example, like tagging images as cat or dog. It can be done by hand, with tools like Label Studio, or partly automated with an existing model.
fact:364: Split your data into a training set to learn from, a validation set to tune settings, and a test set used only once at the end. A common split is 80 percent, 10 percent and 10 percent.
fact:365: Data augmentation creates new training examples by changing existing ones, such as flipping or cropping images, or adding typos and filler words to text. I was trained this way to handle messy questions.
fact:366: Features are the input values a model uses. Feature engineering means creating useful inputs from raw data, like turning a date into day of week, or text into word counts.
fact:367: Feature scaling puts inputs on similar ranges, for example by standardizing to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. It helps many models, especially neural networks and distance based models, train better.
fact:368: Imbalanced data means some classes have far more examples than others. Fixes include collecting more minority data, oversampling, undersampling, class weights in the loss, and judging with precision, recall and F1 instead of accuracy.
fact:369: Data leakage is when information from the test set or the future sneaks into training, making results look better than they really are. Keep the test set separate and only compute preprocessing on training data.
fact:370: Synthetic data is artificially generated training data, made by simulations, rules or other AI models. It helps when real data is scarce or private, but should be checked for quality and realism.
fact:371: A loss function measures how wrong a model's predictions are. Training tries to make the loss smaller. Cross entropy is common for classification and mean squared error for regression.
fact:372: Gradient descent is how most models learn. It computes how the loss changes with each weight, called the gradient, and nudges the weights a small step in the direction that lowers the loss, over and over.
fact:373: Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss for every weight in a neural network by applying the chain rule backward from the output layer to the input layer.
fact:374: The learning rate sets how big each training step is. Too high and training becomes unstable, too low and it is slow. Values around 0.001 are a common start for Adam, often with a schedule that lowers it over time.
fact:375: An epoch is one full pass through the training data. The batch size is how many examples are used in one update step, and each step is called an iteration.
fact:376: An optimizer updates model weights using gradients. SGD takes plain gradient steps, often with momentum. Adam adapts the step size for each weight and is a popular default. AdamW adds proper weight decay.
fact:377: Overfitting is when a model memorizes the training data, including noise, so it scores well in training but poorly on new data.
fact:378: Underfitting is when a model is too simple or trained too little to capture the patterns, so it does poorly on both training and test data. Try a bigger model, better features or longer training.
fact:379: To reduce overfitting: get more data, use data augmentation, add regularization such as weight decay or dropout, use early stopping, simplify the model and use cross validation.
fact:380: Regularization discourages overly complex models. L2 regularization, or weight decay, penalizes large weights, and L1 pushes many weights to exactly zero.
fact:381: Dropout randomly turns off a fraction of neurons during each training step, often 10 to 50 percent, so the network cannot rely on any single neuron. It is turned off at prediction time.
fact:382: Early stopping means watching the validation loss and stopping training when it stops improving, then keeping the best checkpoint. It prevents overfitting and saves time.
fact:383: Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training, like learning rate, batch size and number of layers. Tune them with grid search, random search or Bayesian optimization, judged on the validation set.
fact:384: Parameters, the weights and biases, are the numbers a model learns during training. Weights scale inputs and biases shift outputs. Large language models have billions of them.
fact:385: Activation functions add non-linearity so networks can learn complex patterns. ReLU outputs max of 0 and x and is the common default. Sigmoid squashes values between 0 and 1, and softmax turns scores into probabilities.
fact:386: Normalization layers rescale activations inside a network to keep training stable and fast. Batch normalization is common in CNNs, and layer normalization is used in transformers.
fact:387: Weight initialization sets starting values for weights. Good schemes like Xavier or He initialization scale random values by layer size so signals do not vanish or explode.
fact:388: Vanishing gradients shrink as they flow back through many layers, so early layers stop learning. Exploding gradients grow too large. ReLU, good initialization, normalization, residual connections and gradient clipping help.
fact:389: Cross validation splits data into k parts, trains on k minus 1 parts and tests on the remaining one, rotating k times. Averaging the scores gives a more reliable estimate, especially with small data.
fact:390: High bias means a model is too simple and underfits. High variance means it is too sensitive to training data and overfits. Good models balance the two.
fact:391: A baseline is a simple model, like predicting the most common class or a logistic regression, that sets a minimum score. Any complex model should clearly beat it.
fact:392: Supervised learning trains on labeled examples, input and correct output, such as emails labeled spam or not spam. Classification and regression are supervised tasks.
fact:393: Unsupervised learning finds patterns in unlabeled data, such as grouping customers by behavior with clustering or compressing data with dimensionality reduction.
fact:394: In reinforcement learning, an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from rewards and penalties to maximize total reward. It is used for games, robotics and tuning language models.
fact:395: Self supervised learning creates labels from the data itself, like hiding a word and predicting it. Language models learn this way by predicting the next token in huge amounts of text.
fact:396: Classification predicts a category, like spam or not spam. Regression predicts a number, like a house price.
fact:397: Clustering groups similar data points without labels. K-means picks k centers, assigns each point to its nearest center, moves centers to the average of their points, and repeats.
fact:398: A decision tree splits data with yes or no questions. A random forest averages many trees trained on random samples. Gradient boosting, like XGBoost or LightGBM, adds trees one by one to fix earlier errors and is very strong on tabular data.
fact:399: Linear regression fits a straight line, or plane, that predicts a number from inputs by minimizing squared error. It is the simplest regression model.
fact:400: Logistic regression is a classification model that applies a sigmoid to a weighted sum of inputs to output a probability. It is a strong simple baseline.
fact:401: K nearest neighbors predicts by finding the k most similar training examples and taking a vote or average of their labels. It needs no training but can be slow on big data.
fact:402: A support vector machine finds the boundary that separates classes with the widest margin. Kernels let it learn curved boundaries.
fact:403: A perceptron is the simplest artificial neuron: it multiplies inputs by weights, adds a bias and outputs 1 or 0. Frank Rosenblatt introduced it in 1958.
fact:404: A multilayer perceptron is a feedforward network of fully connected, or dense, layers with activation functions between them. My brain uses this kind of network.
fact:405: A convolutional neural network slides small learned filters across an image to detect edges, textures and shapes, building up to whole objects. CNNs are standard for image tasks.
fact:406: A recurrent neural network processes sequences one step at a time while keeping a memory of earlier steps. LSTMs and GRUs are RNN types that remember longer. Transformers have mostly replaced them.
fact:407: A transformer is a neural network built on self-attention, introduced in the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need. It processes all tokens in parallel and powers modern language models like GPT and Claude.
fact:408: Attention lets each token look at every other token and decide which ones matter most, using query, key and value vectors. Self-attention is the core of transformers.
fact:409: An embedding is a list of numbers, a vector, that represents something like a word or image so similar things have similar vectors. Models learn embeddings during training.
fact:410: Tokenization splits text into pieces called tokens, which can be words, parts of words or characters. Most language models use subword methods like byte pair encoding.
fact:411: An autoencoder compresses input into a small representation with an encoder, then rebuilds it with a decoder. It is used for compression, denoising and anomaly detection.
fact:412: A generative adversarial network has two networks: a generator that makes fake data and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. Competing makes the generator produce realistic results.
fact:413: A diffusion model learns to remove noise step by step. To generate an image, it starts from pure noise and gradually denoises it, often guided by a text prompt.
fact:414: A mixture of experts model has many expert sub-networks and a router that sends each token to only a few of them, so the model can be very large while staying fast.
fact:415: The context window is how many tokens a language model can consider at once, including your prompt and its answer. Modern models range from thousands to over a million tokens.
fact:416: An n-gram model predicts the next word from the previous n minus 1 words using counts. Kneser-Ney smoothing shares probability with unseen word combinations. My language model is a trigram model with Kneser-Ney smoothing.
fact:417: Word2vec learns word embeddings by training a small network to predict words from their neighbors, so words used in similar contexts get similar vectors.
fact:418: A residual, or skip, connection adds a layer's input to its output, which lets gradients flow easily and makes very deep networks trainable. ResNet introduced this idea for images.
fact:419: To build an image classifier: gather labeled images in folders per class, resize and augment them, start from a pretrained CNN or vision transformer like ResNet, replace the final layer with your classes, fine-tune it in PyTorch, and check accuracy on a test set.
fact:420: For a simple chatbot like me: define intents and responses, train a text classifier to recognize intents, and map each intent to a reply. For an advanced chatbot, call or fine-tune a large language model and add retrieval so it can use your documents.
fact:421: To build a large language model: collect and filter a huge text dataset, train a tokenizer, build a transformer, pretrain it to predict the next token on many GPUs, then fine-tune it on instructions and align it with human feedback, and evaluate it on benchmarks.
fact:422: For sentiment analysis: collect text labeled positive, negative or neutral, turn it into features with TF-IDF or a pretrained transformer, train a classifier like logistic regression or a fine-tuned BERT model, and measure F1. You can try a small one here with /build.
fact:423: Recommendation systems use collaborative filtering, which suggests items liked by similar users, content based filtering, which suggests items similar to ones you liked, or hybrids with neural networks and embeddings.
fact:424: To build a spam filter: collect emails labeled spam or not, convert text to word features, train Naive Bayes or logistic regression, then tune the threshold so few real emails get flagged.
fact:425: Speech recognition turns audio into spectrograms and trains a neural network, often a transformer like Whisper, to output text. Fine-tuning a pretrained model is the practical route.
fact:426: An AI agent is a language model that can plan and use tools, like search, code or APIs, in a loop: think, act, observe the result, repeat. You build one by giving the model tool definitions and running that loop.
fact:427: To build a text classifier: gather texts with category labels, turn them into features such as word counts, TF-IDF or embeddings, train a model such as logistic regression or a neural network, and test it. My brain is a text classifier, and /build makes a new one from your data.
fact:428: To predict prices: collect past examples with features like size and location and the price, clean and scale them, train a regression model such as gradient boosting, and measure mean absolute error on a test set.
fact:429: Game playing AIs usually use reinforcement learning, where the agent plays many games and learns from wins and losses, often combined with search. AlphaGo combined neural networks with Monte Carlo tree search.
fact:430: To train on your own data: put it in a table of inputs and labels, split it, and train with scikit-learn or fine-tune a pretrained model. Here you can save a CSV with text,label columns and run /build name path.csv.
fact:431: Object detection finds and boxes objects in images. Models like YOLO or DETR are trained on images labeled with bounding boxes, usually by fine-tuning a pretrained detector.
fact:432: Anomaly detection flags unusual data, like fraud. Common methods are isolation forests, autoencoders that fail to rebuild odd inputs, and classifiers trained on labeled fraud examples.
fact:433: Pretraining is the first big training stage, where a model learns general patterns from huge amounts of data, like predicting the next word in internet text. A pretrained model can then be adapted to specific tasks.
fact:434: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on a smaller, task specific dataset with a low learning rate, so it adapts to your task while keeping what it already learned.
fact:435: Transfer learning reuses knowledge from a model trained on one task for another task, such as fine-tuning an ImageNet model to recognize plant diseases. It saves data and compute.
fact:436: LoRA, low rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small added matrices while freezing the original weights. It needs far less memory. QLoRA does this on a quantized model.
fact:437: RLHF trains a reward model from human preferences between answers, then uses reinforcement learning to make the language model produce answers people prefer. Methods like DPO learn from preferences more directly.
fact:438: Instruction tuning, or supervised fine-tuning, trains a pretrained model on examples of instructions paired with good responses, so it learns to follow requests.
fact:439: Prompt engineering is writing inputs that get better results from a model: be clear and specific, give context and examples, describe the format you want, and break big tasks into steps.
fact:440: Retrieval augmented generation finds relevant documents for a question, usually with embeddings and a vector database, and adds them to the prompt so the model answers from that information. My TF-IDF retriever is a simple form of retrieval.
fact:441: A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the most similar ones. Examples include FAISS, Pinecone, Chroma, Weaviate, Qdrant and pgvector.
fact:442: Quantization stores model weights with fewer bits, like 8 or 4 bits instead of 16 or 32, making models smaller and faster with a small loss in quality.
fact:443: Distillation trains a small student model to copy the outputs of a large teacher model, giving much of the quality at a fraction of the size.
fact:444: Pruning removes weights or neurons that contribute little, making a model smaller and faster, usually followed by a short retraining.
fact:445: Scaling laws show that language model loss falls predictably as you increase model size, data and compute. Compute optimal training balances parameters and tokens.
fact:446: Language models pick each next token from a probability distribution. Temperature controls randomness: low is focused, high is creative. Top-k and top-p sampling limit choices to the most likely tokens. My /generate uses temperature and top-k.
fact:447: Hallucination is when a model states false information confidently. Reduce it with retrieval from trusted sources, asking for citations, better training data and letting the model say I do not know, like I do.
fact:448: Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by text. Lower is better. My language model gives real sentences a perplexity of about 4 and scrambled word salad over 800.
fact:449: Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct. Recall is the share of real positives the model found. F1 is their harmonic mean, useful for imbalanced data.
fact:450: Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct. It can mislead on imbalanced data: if 99 percent of emails are not spam, always guessing not spam gets 99 percent accuracy.
fact:451: A confusion matrix is a table of predicted versus actual classes, showing true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives, so you can see exactly which mistakes a model makes.
fact:452: An ROC curve plots true positive rate against false positive rate across thresholds. AUC, the area under it, summarizes performance: 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is random guessing.
fact:453: For regression, mean squared error averages squared differences between predictions and true values, and mean absolute error averages absolute differences, which is easier to interpret.
fact:454: Evaluate on a held-out test set the model never trained on, using metrics that match your goal, compare against a baseline, look at a confusion matrix and real mistakes, and test on messy real world inputs.
fact:455: A benchmark is a standard test set for comparing models, such as ImageNet for images, or MMLU, GPQA and SWE-bench for language models.
fact:456: PyTorch is a popular open source deep learning framework from Meta. It builds networks in plain Python with automatic gradients and runs on GPUs. It is the most common choice in research.
fact:457: TensorFlow is Google's deep learning framework, used widely in production. Keras is its easy high level API for building networks layer by layer.
fact:458: JAX is a Google library for fast numerical computing with automatic gradients and compilation for GPUs and TPUs. It is popular for large scale research.
fact:459: Scikit-learn is a Python library for classic machine learning: regression, classification, clustering, preprocessing and evaluation. It is the best place to start for tabular data.
fact:460: NumPy provides fast arrays and math in Python, and I am built on it. Pandas provides data tables, called DataFrames, for loading and cleaning data.
fact:461: Hugging Face is a platform and set of libraries for sharing and using AI models and datasets. Its Transformers library lets you load thousands of pretrained models in a few lines of Python.
fact:462: A Jupyter notebook mixes code, results and notes in one document. Google Colab runs notebooks in the cloud with free GPU access, which is great for learning.
fact:463: Small models, like me, train fine on a laptop CPU. Deep learning on images or text is much faster on a GPU, because GPUs do thousands of calculations in parallel. Free cloud GPUs are a good start.
fact:464: CUDA is NVIDIA's platform for running computations on its GPUs, which most AI training uses. TPUs are Google's chips designed specifically for machine learning.
fact:465: To deploy a model: save it, wrap it in an API with FastAPI or Flask, package it in a Docker container and run it on a server or cloud service. Libraries like ONNX Runtime or vLLM make serving faster.
fact:466: MLOps is the practice of reliably deploying, monitoring and updating models. Model drift is when real data changes over time so accuracy drops, which is why you monitor and retrain.
fact:467: Save a model's learned weights to a file, called a checkpoint, and load them later. In PyTorch use torch.save and load_state_dict. I save my brain as brain.npz and my language model as lm.pkl.
fact:468: Training is when a model learns its weights. Inference is when the trained model makes predictions on new inputs.
fact:469: Experiment tracking records settings, metrics and results of each training run so you can compare them. Popular tools are MLflow and Weights and Biases.
fact:470: ONNX is an open format for AI models. You can export a model from PyTorch or TensorFlow to ONNX and run it fast with ONNX Runtime on many devices.
fact:471:
Here is a small PyTorch network:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(10, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 2))
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()
for x, y in loader:
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(model(x), y)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

print(clf.predict(['great product']))
fact:474: AI bias is when a model treats groups unfairly, often because of skewed training data. Reduce it with diverse data, testing results per group, fairness metrics and human review.
fact:475: AI safety and alignment aim to make AI systems helpful, honest and harmless, doing what people intend. Methods include careful data, human feedback training, red teaming and safety evaluations before release.
fact:476: Red teaming means deliberately trying to make a model fail or misbehave, so problems can be found and fixed before release.
fact:477: A model card documents a model: what it is for, the data it was trained on, its performance, its limits and known risks.
fact:478: Protect privacy by collecting only needed data, removing personal details, getting consent, securing storage, and using methods like differential privacy or federated learning.
